title: Indigo
summary: Louis Fischer narrates how Gandhi, at the persistent request of a poor peasant named Rajkumar Shukla, went to Champaran in Bihar in 1917 to investigate the exploitation of indigo sharecroppers by British planters. Through peaceful defiance and patient negotiation he won the peasants a partial refund and, more importantly, the courage to stand up for themselves.

notes.heading: About the author
notes.html: Louis Fischer (1896–1970) was an American journalist who met Gandhi in 1942 and wrote The Life of Mahatma Gandhi, on which the film Gandhi was based. The chapter is an excerpt from that biography.

notes.heading: Gist
notes.html: Rajkumar Shukla, an illiterate sharecropper, met Gandhi at the Lucknow session of the Congress in December 1916 and followed him until he agreed to visit Champaran. There Gandhi found that peasants were forced under a long-term agreement to grow indigo on fifteen per cent of their land and hand the crop over as rent. When synthetic indigo made the crop unprofitable, planters demanded compensation for releasing peasants. Gandhi defied an order to leave, faced trial, and led an inquiry that ended in a settlement refunding twenty-five per cent of the money. He called Champaran the turning point in his life.

notes.heading: Detailed summary
notes.html:
Shukla’s persistence. Gandhi told Fischer how Shukla, a poor, emaciated peasant, followed him from Lucknow to Cawnpore and to his ashram near Ahmedabad until Gandhi named a date. In Calcutta, Shukla waited until Gandhi was free, and the two took a train to Patna.

Patna and Muzaffarpur. Shukla took Gandhi to the house of lawyer Rajendra Prasad, who was away. The servants, thinking Gandhi just another peasant, did not let him draw water from the well. Gandhi went to Muzaffarpur, where Professor J. B. Kripalani received him with students. He was surprised that a Briton-ruled people welcomed someone who supported Home Rule. Lawyers there told him about peasants’ cases in court; Gandhi scolded them for taking high fees and said the real relief lay in freeing the peasants from fear, not in law courts.

The sharecropping system. Most arable land in Champaran was owned by English planters and worked by Indian tenants. The main crop was indigo. Under a long-term contract, tenants had to plant fifteen per cent of their holdings with indigo and surrender the harvest as rent. When Germany developed synthetic indigo, planters got the peasants to sign agreements paying compensation to be released from the fifteen per cent arrangement. Some peasants who later understood the trick wanted their money back.

Defiance at Motihari. Gandhi went to the British Commissioner, who bullied him and told him to leave Tirhut. Gandhi instead went to Motihari, the district capital. On the way to investigate a peasant’s mistreatment, he was served with an official notice to quit Champaran. He signed the receipt and wrote that he would disobey. He was summoned to court. Thousands of peasants gathered spontaneously outside. The officials, nervous, needed Gandhi’s help to control the crowd. In court he stated that he was obeying a higher law of conscience and was ready to accept the penalty. The judge postponed judgment and later the case was dropped. This was the first triumph of civil disobedience in modern India.

The inquiry and settlement. With lawyers including Rajendra Prasad, who decided to stay and even go to jail, Gandhi recorded the grievances of about ten thousand peasants. The Lieutenant-Governor set up a commission. Gandhi demanded fifty per cent refund but agreed to twenty-five per cent, explaining that the amount mattered less than the fact that the planters had been forced to surrender both money and prestige. Within a few years the planters left the estates, which reverted to the peasants, and indigo sharecropping disappeared.

Social work and self-reliance. Gandhi did not stop at politics. With volunteers, including his wife Kasturba and his son, he opened primary schools in six villages, arranged a doctor, and taught hygiene. When his friends suggested that the Englishman C. F. Andrews stay on to help, Gandhi refused, saying that relying on an Englishman showed weakness and that they must learn to depend on themselves.

notes.heading: Themes
notes.html:
• Freedom from fear: Gandhi’s greatest gift to the peasants was courage.
  • Non-violent resistance: civil disobedience as a moral and practical weapon.
  • Self-reliance: Indians must not depend on outsiders, even well-meaning ones.
  • Leadership through service: politics linked with the everyday needs of the poor.
  • Exploitation under colonial rule: the unjust sharecropping system.

notes.heading: Character sketches
notes.html:
Gandhi: humble, practical and morally firm. He listens to a poor peasant, studies facts before acting, defies unjust orders peacefully, compromises wisely, and attends to education and health. He sees freedom from fear as the root of independence.

Rajkumar Shukla: illiterate but resolute; his persistence brings Gandhi to Champaran and starts the movement.

Rajendra Prasad and the lawyers: they evolve from fee-charging professionals to committed volunteers ready to court arrest.

notes.heading: Title justification
notes.html: Indigo, the crop at the heart of the peasants’ exploitation, gives the chapter its name. The struggle around it became a symbol of the end of colonial economic oppression and the beginning of Gandhi’s mass movement in India.

notes.heading: Message and values
notes.html: Injustice can be resisted through truth, courage and non-violence. True leadership empowers people to stand on their own feet, and freedom begins when people stop being afraid.

keyTerms.definition: A tenant farmer who gives a share of the crop to the landowner as rent.
The arrangement compelling Champaran peasants to grow indigo on three-twentieths (15%) of their land for the planters.
Artificial dye developed in Germany that made natural indigo unprofitable.
Peaceful refusal to obey unjust laws while accepting the penalty; first used by Gandhi in India at Motihari.
Senior British official of the Tirhut division who ordered Gandhi to leave.
Self-government for India within the British Empire.
Depending on one’s own strength; the reason Gandhi did not want C. F. Andrews to stay.
Return of money; the planters agreed to return 25% of what they had extracted.

mcqs.q: Where did Rajkumar Shukla first meet Gandhi?
options: At the Lucknow session of the Indian National Congress
mcqs.explanation: Shukla met Gandhi at the Lucknow Congress session in December 1916 and then followed him for months.

mcqs.q: Under the sharecropping arrangement, the peasants had to plant indigo on:
mcqs.explanation: They had to grow indigo on fifteen per cent of their holdings and hand it over as rent.

mcqs.q: Why did the planters want to release the peasants from the indigo agreement?
options: Germany had developed synthetic indigo, making the crop unprofitable.
mcqs.explanation: Synthetic indigo from Germany made natural indigo worthless, so planters extracted compensation for releasing tenants.

mcqs.q: Why did Rajendra Prasad’s servants not let Gandhi draw water from the well?
options: They thought he was an untouchable peasant.
mcqs.explanation: Seeing his simple clothes and Shukla’s company, they took him for another untouchable peasant.

mcqs.q: What did Gandhi do on receiving the order to leave Champaran?
options: He signed the receipt and wrote that he would disobey it.
mcqs.explanation: He signed for the notice and wrote on it that he would disobey, an act of peaceful defiance.

mcqs.q: Why did the officials need Gandhi’s help at the Motihari court?
options: They could not control the huge crowd of peasants.
They wanted him as a lawyer.
mcqs.explanation: Thousands of peasants gathered spontaneously and the officials were powerless without Gandhi’s cooperation.

mcqs.q: Why did Gandhi accept a 25% refund instead of 50%?
options: The amount mattered less than the planters’ surrender of prestige.
mcqs.explanation: For Gandhi, the planters’ loss of prestige and admission of wrong were more important than the sum.

mcqs.q: Why did Gandhi not want C. F. Andrews to stay in Champaran?
options: Depending on an Englishman showed weakness; Indians had to be self-reliant.
mcqs.explanation: Gandhi wanted the movement to be self-reliant; seeking an Englishman’s support betrayed weakness.
Professor J. B. Kripalani of the Arts College met him with a large group of students.

mcqs.q: Which of the following social measures did Gandhi undertake in Champaran?
options: Opening primary schools and arranging medical help
mcqs.explanation: He opened schools in six villages, brought a doctor and taught hygiene, showing his concern for overall welfare.

questions.q:
Read the situation and answer: At Motihari, Gandhi tells the court that he is disobeying the order not out of disrespect for authority but in obedience to a higher law of conscience, and that he is ready to accept the penalty.
(a) Which order is he disobeying? (1)
(b) What is the ‘higher law’ he refers to? (1)
(c) What is this form of protest called? (1)
(d) How did the case end? (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) The official order to leave Champaran.

(b) The voice of his conscience, his moral duty to help the peasants.

(c) Civil disobedience.

(d) The judge postponed the verdict and the case was later dropped.

questions.q: Why did Gandhi feel it was useless for the peasants to go to law courts?
questions.answerHtml: Gandhi felt the peasants were crushed and fear-stricken, and the lawyers charged them heavy fees. Court cases brought little relief. The real need was to free them from fear and make them confident enough to stand up to the planters.

questions.q: Why did Gandhi call the Champaran episode a turning point in his life?
questions.answerHtml: At Champaran, the ordinary peasants defied the British for the first time through civil disobedience, proving that non-violent resistance could work. It also showed Gandhi that freeing Indians from fear was the key to independence. It shaped his later mass movements.

questions.q: How did the lawyers’ attitude change during the Champaran movement?
questions.answerHtml: At first the lawyers were ready to return home if Gandhi went to jail. Seeing a stranger ready to suffer for their peasants, they felt ashamed. They decided to follow Gandhi, record the peasants’ grievances, and court arrest if needed.

questions.q: ‘Freedom from fear is more important than legal justice for the poor.’ Do you agree? Discuss with reference to ‘Indigo’. (120–150 words)
questions.answerHtml:
Yes, ‘Indigo’ shows that fearlessness matters more to the poor than legal relief. The Champaran peasants had long been crushed by British planters and had simply submitted. Court cases cost them heavy fees and changed nothing, because they remained too afraid to resist.

Gandhi understood that the real disease was fear. When he openly defied the order to leave Champaran and calmly faced trial, thousands of peasants gathered outside the court in support. For the first time they saw a man stand up to authority without violence, and they lost their fear.

This courage was more valuable than the 25% refund. Gandhi himself said the planters’ surrender of prestige mattered more than money. Within a few years the planters left and the land returned to the peasants. Thus, once the poor stopped being afraid, justice followed. Freedom from fear became the foundation of India’s struggle for freedom.

questions.q: Gandhi’s politics was closely linked with the day-to-day problems of the people. Justify with reference to ‘Indigo’. (120–150 words)
questions.answerHtml:
Gandhi’s politics in Champaran grew directly from the everyday sufferings of ordinary people. He went there not for a grand cause but because a poor peasant, Rajkumar Shukla, begged him to see the injustice of indigo sharecropping. He studied the facts patiently, recorded the statements of thousands of peasants and negotiated a refund of their money.

He did not stop at winning the case. Noticing the villagers’ poverty and backwardness, he opened primary schools in six villages, with his wife Kasturba and volunteers as teachers. He arranged for a doctor and medicines, and taught cleanliness and hygiene to improve health.

He also taught self-reliance, refusing to depend on C. F. Andrews. For Gandhi, independence meant not just removing British rule but improving the daily lives of Indians. His political struggle thus became a movement of social reform, combining justice, education and self-respect.
